entries.7e04c3a73e08938621d229804a768b12db8b6cc2: <div sID="gen4406" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Josh.15" sID="Josh.15"/> <div eID="gen4406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4407" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4408" type="x-p"/> Though the land was not completely conquered, yet being (as was said in the close of the foregoing chapter) as rest from war for the present, and their armies all drawn out of the field to a general rendezvous at Gilgal, there they began to divide the land, though the work was afterwards perfected at Shiloh, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.1-Josh.18.10">ch. xviii. 1</reference>, &c. In this chapter we have the lot of the tribe of Judah, which in this, as in other things, had the precedency. I. The borders or bounds of the inheritance of Judah, <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1-Josh.16.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. II. The particular assignment of Hebron and the country thereabout to Caleb and his family, <reference osisRef="Josh.16.13-Josh.16.19">ver. 13-19</reference>. III. The names of the several cities that fell within Judah's lot, <reference osisRef="Josh.16.20-Josh.16.63">ver. 20-63</reference>.
entries.ccdb201350d629b9f61d5153e84b26837da5280f: <div eID="gen4408" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4407" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lot of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="italic">This</hi> then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families; <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward <hi type="italic">was</hi> the uttermost part of the south coast. <hi type="super">2</hi> And their south border was from the shore of the salt sea, from the bay that looketh southward: <hi type="super">3</hi> And it went out to the south side to Maaleh-acrabbim, and passed along to Zin, and ascended up on the south side unto Kadesh-barnea, and passed along to Hezron, and went up to Adar, and fetched a compass to Karkaa: <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">From thence</hi> it passed toward Azmon, and went out unto the river of Egypt; and the goings out of that coast were at the sea: this shall be your south coast. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the east border <hi type="italic">was</hi> the salt sea, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the end of Jordan. And <hi type="italic">their</hi> border in the north quarter <hi type="italic">was</hi> from the bay of the sea at the uttermost part of Jordan: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the border went up to Beth-hogla, and passed along by the north of Beth-arabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben: <hi type="super">7</hi> And the border went up toward Debir from the valley of Achor, and so northward, looking toward Gilgal, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> before the going up to Adummim, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the south side of the river: and the border passed toward the waters of En-shemesh, and the goings out thereof were at En-rogel: <hi type="super">8</hi> And the border went up by the valley of the son of Hinnom unto the south side of the Jebusite; the same <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jerusalem: and the border went up to the top of the mountain that <hi type="italic">lieth</hi> before the valley of Hinnom westward, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at the end of the valley of the giants northward: <hi type="super">9</hi> And the border was drawn from the top of the hill unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of mount Ephron; and the border was drawn to Baalah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Kirjath-jearim: <hi type="super">10</hi> And the border compassed from Baalah westward unto mount Seir, and passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Chesalon, on the north side, and went down to Beth-shemesh, and passed on to Timnah: <hi type="super">11</hi> And the border went out unto the side of Ekron northward: and the border was drawn to Shicron, and passed along to mount Baalah, and went out unto Jabneel; and the goings out of the border were at the sea. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the west border <hi type="italic">was</hi> to the great sea, and the coast <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the coast of the children of Judah round about according to their families. <div eID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4410" type="x-p"/> Judah and Joseph were the two sons of Jacob on whom Reuben's forfeited birth-right devolved. Judah had the dominion entailed on him, and Joseph the double portion, and therefore these two tribes were first seated, Judah in the southern part of the land of Canaan and Joseph in the northern part, and on them the other seven did attend, and had their respective lots as appurtenances to these two; the lots of Benjamin, Simeon, and Dan, were appendant to Judah, and those of Issachar and Zebulun, Naphtali and Asher, to Joseph. These two were first set up to be provided for, it should seem, before there was such an exact survey of the land as we find afterwards, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.9">ch. xviii. 9</reference>. It is probable that the most considerable parts of the northern and southern countries, and those that lay nearest to Gilgal, and which the people were best acquainted with, were first put into two portions, and the lot was cast upon them between these two principal tribes, of the one of which Joshua was, and of the other Caleb, who was the first commissioner in this writ of partition; and, by the decision of that lot, the southern country, of which we have an account in this chapter, fell to Judah, and the northern, of which we have an account in the two following chapters, to Joseph. And when this was done there was a more equal dividend (either in quantity or quality) of the remainder among the seven tribes. And this, probably, was intended in that general rule which was given concerning this partition (<reference osisRef="Num.33.54">Num. xxxiii. 54</reference>), <hi type="italic">to the more you shall give the more inheritance, and to the fewer you shall give the less,</hi> and <hi type="italic">every man's inheritance shall be where his lot falleth;</hi> that is, "You shall appoint two greater portions which shall be determined by lot to those more numerous tribes of Judah and Joseph, and then the rest shall be less portions to be allotted to the less numerous tribes." The former was done in Gilgal, the latter in Shiloh. <div eID="gen4410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4411" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have the borders of the lot of Judah, which, as the rest, is said to be <hi type="italic">by their families,</hi> that is, with an eye to the number of their families. And it intimates that Joshua and Eleazar, and the rest of the commissioners, when they had by lot given each tribe its portion, did afterwards (it is probable by lot likewise) subdivide those larger portions, and assign to each family its inheritance, and then to each household, which would be better done by this supreme authority, and be apt to give less disgust than if it had been left to the inferior magistrates of each tribe to make that distribution. The borders of this tribe are here largely fixed, yet not unalterably, for a good deal of that which lies within these bounds was afterwards assigned to the lots of Simeon and <reference osisRef="Dan.1">Dan. 1</reference>. The eastern border was all, and only, the Salt Sea, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5">v. 5</reference>. Every sea is salt, but this was of an extraordinary and more than natural saltness, the effects of that fire and brimstone with which Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed in Abraham's time, whose ruins lie buried in the bottom of this dead water, which never either was moved itself or had any living thing in it. 2. The southern border was that of the land of Canaan in general, as will appear by comparing <reference osisRef="Josh.15.1-Josh.15.4 Num.15.34 Num.3">v. 1-4 with Num. xxxiv. 3-5</reference>. So that this powerful and warlike tribe of Judah guarded the frontiers of the whole land, on that side which lay towards their old sworn enemies (though their two fathers were twin-brethren), the Edomites. Our Lord therefore, who <hi type="italic">sprang out of Judah,</hi> and whose <hi type="italic">the kingdom is, shall judge the mount of Esau,</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.21">Obad. 21</reference>. 3. The northern border divided it from the lot of Benjamin. In this, mention is made of <hi type="italic">the stone of Bohan</hi> a Reubenite (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">v. 6</reference>), who probably was a great commander of those forces of Reuben that came over Jordan, and died in the camp at Gilgal, and was buried not far off under this stone. The valley of Achor likewise lies upon this border (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.7">v. 7</reference>), to remind the men of Judah of the trouble which Achan, one of their tribe, gave to the congregation of Israel, that they might not be too much lifted up with their services. This northern line touched closely upon Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.8">v. 8</reference>), so closely as to include in the lot of this tribe Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, though the greater part of the city lay in the lot of Benjamin. 4. The west border went near to the great sea at first (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.12">v. 12</reference>), but afterwards the lot of the tribe of Dan took off a good part of Judah's lot on that side; for the lot was only to determine between Judah and Joseph, which should have the north and which the south, and not immovably to fix the border of either. Judah's inheritance had its boundaries determined. Though it was a powerful warlike tribe, and had a great interest in the other tribes, yet they must not therefore be left to their own choice, to enlarge their possessions at pleasure, but must live so as that their neighbours might live by them. Those that are placed high yet must not think to be <hi type="italic">placed alone in the midst of the earth.</hi>
entries.168974904643a203bbf323b7ddbf1e42c3f0f6c3: <div eID="gen4411" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Caleb's Inheritance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4412" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh he gave a part among the children of Judah, according to the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to Joshua, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the city of Arba the father of Anak, which <hi type="italic">city is</hi> Hebron. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he went up thence to the inhabitants of Debir: and the name of Debir before <hi type="italic">was</hi> Kirjath-sepher. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjath-sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife. <hi type="super">18</hi> And it came to pass, as she came <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted off <hi type="italic">her</hi> ass; and Caleb said unto her, What wouldest thou? <hi type="super">19</hi> Who answered, Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs. <div eID="gen4412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4413" type="x-p"/> The historian seems pleased with every occasion to make mention of Caleb and to do him honour, because he had honoured God in following him fully. Observe, <div eID="gen4413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4414" type="x-p"/> I. The grant Joshua made him of the mountain of Hebron for his inheritance is here repeated (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.13">v. 13</reference>), and it is said to be given him. 1. <hi type="italic">According to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua.</hi> Though Caleb, in his petition, had made out a very good title to it by promise, yet, because God had ordered Joshua to divide the land by lot, he would not in this one single instance, no, not to gratify his old friend Caleb, do otherwise, without orders from God, whose oracle, it is probable, he consulted upon this occasion. In every doubtful case it is very desirable to know the mind of God, and to see the way of our duty plain. 2. It is said to be a part <hi type="italic">among the children of Judah;</hi> though it was assigned him before the lot of that tribe came up, yet it proved, God so directing the lot, to be in the heart of that tribe, which was graciously ordered in kindness to him, that he might not be as one separated from his brethren and surrounded by those of other tribes. <div eID="gen4414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4415" type="x-p"/> II. Caleb having obtained this grant, we are told, <div eID="gen4415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4416" type="x-p"/> 1. How he signalized his own valour in the conquest of Hebron (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">He drove thence the three sons of Anak,</hi> he and those that he engaged to assist him in this service. This is mentioned here to show that the confidence he had expressed of success in this affair, through the presence of God with him (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.12">ch. xiv. 12</reference>), did not deceive him, but the event answered his expectation. It is not said that he <hi type="italic">slew these giants,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">drove them thence,</hi> which intimates that they retired upon his approach and fled before him; the strength and stature of their bodies could not keep up the courage of their minds, but with the countenances of lions they had the hearts of trembling hares. Thus does God often <hi type="italic">cut off the spirit of princes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.12">Ps. lxxvi. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">take away the heart of the chief of the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job xii. 24</reference>), and so shame the confidence of the proud; and thus if we resist the devil, that roaring lion, though he fall not, yet he will flee. <div eID="gen4416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4417" type="x-p"/> 2. How he encouraged the valour of those about him in the conquest of Debir, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.15-Josh.15.19">v. 15</reference>, &c. It seems, though Joshua had once made himself master of Debir (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.39">ch. x. 39</reference>), yet the Canaanites had regained the possession in the absence of the army, so that the work had to be done a second time; and when Caleb had completed the reduction of Hebron, which was for himself and his own family, to show his zeal for the public good, as much as for his own private interest, he pushes on his conquest to Debir, and will not lay down his arms till he sees that city also effectually reduced, which lay but ten miles southward from Hebron, though he had not any particular concern in it, but the reducing of it would be to the general advantage of his tribe. Let us learn hence not to seek and mind our own things only, but to concern and engage ourselves for the welfare of the community we are members of; we are not born for ourselves, nor must we <hi type="italic">live to ourselves.</hi> <div eID="gen4417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4418" type="x-p"/> (1.) Notice is taken of the name of this city. It had been called <hi type="italic">Kirjath-sepher, the city of a book,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kirjath-sannah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.49">v. 49</reference>), which some translate <hi type="italic">the city of learning</hi> (so the LXX. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Polis grammaton</hi></hi>), whence some conjecture that it had been a university among the Canaanites, like Athens in Greece, in which their youth were educated; or perhaps the books of their chronicles or records, or the antiquities of the nation, were laid up there; and, it may be, this was it that made Caleb so desirous to see Israel master of this city, that they might get acquainted with the ancient learning of the Canaanites. <div eID="gen4418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4419" type="x-p"/> (2.) The proffer that Caleb made of his daughter, and a good portion with her, to any one that would undertake to reduce that city, and to command the forces that should be employed in that service, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.16">v. 16</reference>. Thus Saul promised a daughter to him that would kill Goliath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">1 Sam. xvii. 25</reference>), neither of them intending to force his daughter to marry such as she could not love, but both of them presuming upon their daughters' obedience, and submission to their fathers' will, though it might be contrary to their own humour or inclination. Caleb's family was not long honourable and wealthy, but religious; he that himself <hi type="italic">followed the Lord fully</hi> no doubt taught his children to do so, and therefore it could not but be a desirable match to any young gentleman. Caleb, in making the proposal, aims, [1.] To do service to his country by the reducing of that important place; and, [2.] To marry a daughter well, to a man of learning, that would have a particular affection for <hi type="italic">the city of books,</hi> and a man of war, that would be likely to serve his country, and do worthily in his generation. Could he but marry his child to a man of such a character, he would think her well bestowed, whether the share in the lot of his tribe were more or less. <div eID="gen4419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> (3.) The place was bravely taken by Othniel, a nephew of Caleb, whom probably Caleb had thoughts of when he made the proffer, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.17">v. 17</reference>. This Othniel, who thus signalized himself when he was young, had long after, in his advanced years, the honour to be both a deliverer and a judge in Israel, the first single person that presided in their affairs after Joshua's death. It is good for those who are setting out in the world to begin betimes with that which is great and good, that, excelling in service when they are young, they may excel in honour when they grow old. <div eID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> (4.) Hereupon (all parties being agreed) Othniel married his cousin-german Achsah, Caleb's daughter. It is probable that he had a kindness for her before, which put him upon this bold undertaking to obtain her. Love to his country, an ambition of honour, and a desire to find favour with the princes of his people, might not have engaged him in this great action, but his affection for Achsah did. This made it intolerable to him to think that any one should do more to win her favour than he would, and so inspired him with this generous fire. Thus is love strong as death, and jealousy cruel as the grave. <div eID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> (5.) Because the historian is now upon the dividing of the land, he gives us an account of Achsah's portion, which was in land, as more valuable because enjoyed by virtue of the divine promise, though we may suppose the conquerors of Canaan, who had had the spoil of so many rich cities, were full of money too. [1.] Some land she obtained by Caleb's free grant, which was allowed while she married within her own tribe and family, as Zelophehad's daughters did. He <hi type="italic">gave her a south land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.15.19">v. 19</reference>. Land indeed, but <hi type="italic">a south land,</hi> dry, and apt to be parched. [2.] She obtained more upon her request; she would have had her husband to ask for a field, probably some particular field, or champaign ground, which belonged to Caleb's lot, and joined to that south land which he had settled upon his daughter at marriage. She thought her husband had the best interest in her father, who, no doubt, was extremely pleased with his late glorious achievement, but he thought it was more proper for her to ask, and she would be more likely to prevail; accordingly she did, submitting to her husband's judgment, though contrary to her own; and she managed the undertaking with great address. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She took the opportunity when her father brought her home to the house of her husband, when the satisfaction of having disposed of his daughter so well would make him think nothing too much to do for her. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She <hi type="italic">lighted off her ass,</hi> in token of respect and reverence to her father, whom she would honour still, as much as before her marriage. She <hi type="italic">cried</hi> or <hi type="italic">sighed</hi> from off her ass, so the LXX. and the vulgar Latin read it; she expressed some grief and concern, that she might give her father occasion to ask her what she wanted. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> She calls it <hi type="italic">a blessing,</hi> because it would add much to the comfort of her settlement; and she was sure that, since she married not only with her father's consent, but in obedience to his command, he would not deny her his blessing. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> She asks only for the <hi type="italic">water,</hi> without which the ground she had would be of little use either for tillage or pasture, but she means the field in which the springs of water were. The modesty and reasonableness of her quest gave it a great advantage. Earth without water would be like a tree without sap, or the body of an animal without blood; therefore, when God <hi type="italic">gathered the waters into one place,</hi> he wisely and graciously left some in every place, that the earth might be enriched for the service of man. See <reference osisRef="Ps.104.10-Ps.104.23">Ps. civ. 10</reference>, &c. Well, Achsah gained her point; her father gave her what she asked, and perhaps more, for <hi type="italic">he gave her the upper springs and the nether springs,</hi> two fields so called from the springs that were in them, as we commonly distinguish between the higher field and the lower field. Those who understand it but of one field, watered both with the rain of heaven and the springs that issued out of the bowels of the earth, give countenance to the allusion we commonly make to this, when we pray for spiritual and heavenly blessings which relate to our souls as blessings of the upper springs, and those which relate to the body and the life that now is as blessings of the nether springs. <div eID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> From this story we learn, 1. That it is no breach of the tenth commandment moderately to desire those comforts and conveniences of this life which we see attainable in a fair and regular way. 2. That husbands and wives should mutually advise, and jointly agree, about that which is for the common good of their family; and much more should they concur in asking of their heavenly Father the best blessings, those of the upper springs. 3. That parents must never think that lost which is bestowed upon their children for their real advantage, but must be free in giving them portions as well as maintenance, especially when they are dutiful. Caleb had sons (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.15">1 Chron. iv. 15</reference>), and yet gave thus liberally to his daughter. Those parents forget themselves and their relation who grudge their children what is convenient for them when they can conveniently part with it.
entries.e5a870d36ea190e85b77cd0736b922cfbb134fbd: <div eID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lot of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward were Kabzeel, and Eder, and Jagur, <hi type="super">22</hi> And Kinah, and Dimonah, and Adadah, <hi type="super">23</hi> And Kedesh, and Hazor, and Ithnan, <hi type="super">24</hi> Ziph, and Telem, and Bealoth, <hi type="super">25</hi> And Hazor, Hadattah, and Kerioth, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Hezron, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Hazor, <hi type="super">26</hi> Amam, and Shema, and Moladah, <hi type="super">27</hi> And Hazar-gaddah, and Heshmon, and Beth-palet, <hi type="super">28</hi> And Hazar-shual, and Beer-sheba, and Bizjoth-jah, <hi type="super">29</hi> Baalah, and Iim, and Azem, <hi type="super">30</hi> And Eltolad, and Chesil, and Hormah, <hi type="super">31</hi> And Ziklag, and Madmannah, and Sansannah, <hi type="super">32</hi> And Lebaoth, and Shilhim, and Ain, and Rimmon: all the cities <hi type="italic">are</hi> twenty and nine, with their villages:   33 <hi type="italic">And</hi> in the valley, Eshtaol, and Zoreah, and Ashnah, <hi type="super">34</hi> And Zanoah, and En-gannim, Tappuah, and Enam, <hi type="super">35</hi> Jarmuth, and Adullam, Socoh, and Azekah, <hi type="super">36</hi> And Sharaim, and Adithaim, and Gederah, and Gederothaim; fourteen cities with their villages: <hi type="super">37</hi> Zenan, and Hadashah, and Migdal-gad, <hi type="super">38</hi> And Dilean, and Mizpeh, and Joktheel, <hi type="super">39</hi> Lachish, and Bozkath, and Eglon, <hi type="super">40</hi> And Cabbon, and Lahmam, and Kithlish, <hi type="super">41</hi> And Gederoth, Beth-dagon, and Naamah, and Makkedah; sixteen cities with their villages: <hi type="super">42</hi> Libnah, and Ether, and Ashan, <hi type="super">43</hi> And Jiphtah, and Ashnah, and Nezib, <hi type="super">44</hi> And Keilah, and Achzib, and Mareshah; nine cities with their villages: <hi type="super">45</hi> Ekron, with her towns and her villages: <hi type="super">46</hi> From Ekron even unto the sea, all that <hi type="italic">lay</hi> near Ashdod, with their villages: <hi type="super">47</hi> Ashdod with her towns and her villages, Gaza with her towns and her villages, unto the river of Egypt, and the great sea, and the border <hi type="italic">thereof:</hi> <hi type="super">48</hi> And in the mountains, Shamir, and Jattir, and Socoh, <hi type="super">49</hi> And Dannah, and Kirjath-sannah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Debir, <hi type="super">50</hi> And Anab, and Eshtemoh, and Anim, <hi type="super">51</hi> And Goshen, and Holon, and Giloh; eleven cities with their villages: <hi type="super">52</hi> Arab, and Dumah, and Eshean, <hi type="super">53</hi> And Janum, and Beth-tappuah, and Aphekah, <hi type="super">54</hi> And Humtah, and Kirjath-arba, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Hebron, and Zior; nine cities with their villages: <hi type="super">55</hi> Maon, Carmel, and Ziph, and Juttah, <hi type="super">56</hi> And Jezreel, and Jokdeam, and Zanoah, <hi type="super">57</hi> Cain, Gibeah, and Timnah; ten cities with their villages: <hi type="super">58</hi> Halhul, Beth-zur, and Gedor, <hi type="super">59</hi> And Maarath, and Beth-anoth, and Eltekon; six cities with their villages: <hi type="super">60</hi> Kirjath-baal, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Kirjath-jearim, and Rabbah; two cities with their villages: <hi type="super">61</hi> In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, and Secacah, <hi type="super">62</hi> And Nibshan, and the city of Salt, and En-gedi; six cities with their villages. <hi type="super">63</hi> As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day. <div eID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> We have here a list of the several cities that fell within the lot of the tribe of Judah, which are mentioned by name, that they might know their own, and both keep it and keep to it, and might neither through cowardice nor sloth lose the possession of what was their own. <div eID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> I. The cities are here named, and numbered in several classes, which they then could account for the reason of better than we can now. Here are, 1. Some that are said to be the uttermost cities <hi type="italic">towards the coast of Edom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">v. 21-32</reference>. Here are thirty-eight named, and yet said to be <hi type="italic">twenty-nine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.32">v. 32</reference>), because nine of these were afterwards transferred to the lot of Simeon, and are reckoned as belonging to that, as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="Josh.19.2-Josh.19.9">ch. xix. 2</reference>, &c.; therefore those only are counted (though the rest are named) which remained to Judah. 2. Others that are said to be <hi type="italic">in the valley</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.33">v. 33</reference>) are counted to be fourteen, yet fifteen are named; but it is probable that Gederah and Gederathaim were either two names or two parts of one and the same city. 3. Then sixteen are named without any head of distinction, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.37-Josh.15.41">v. 37-41</reference>, and nine more, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.42-Josh.15.44">v. 42-44</reference>. 4. Then the three Philistine-cities, Ekron, Ashdod, and Gaza, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.45-Josh.15.47">v. 45-47</reference>. 5. Cities <hi type="italic">in the mountains,</hi> eleven in all (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.48-Josh.15.51">v. 48-51</reference>), nine more (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.52-Josh.15.54">v. 52-54</reference>), ten more (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.55-Josh.15.57">v. 55-57</reference>), six more (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.58-Josh.15.59">v. 58, 59</reference>), then two (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.60">v. 60</reference>), and six in the wilderness, a part of the country not so thick of inhabitants as some others were. <div eID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4427" type="x-p"/> II. Now here, 1. We do not find Bethlehem, which was afterwards the city of David, and was ennobled by the birth of our Lord Jesus in it. But that city, which at the best was but <hi type="italic">little among the thousands of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>), except that it was thus dignified, was now so little as not to be accounted one of the cities, but perhaps was one of the villages not named. Christ came to give honour to the places he was related to, not to receive honour from them. 2. Jerusalem is said to continue in the hands of the Jebusites (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">v. 63</reference>), <hi type="italic">for the children of Judah could not drive them out,</hi> through their sluggishness, stupidity, and unbelief. Had they attempted it with vigour and resolution, we have reason to think God would not have been wanting to them to give them success; but they could not do it, because they would not. Jerusalem was afterwards to be the holy city, the royal city, the city of the great King, the brightest ornament of all the land of Israel. God has designed it should be so. It may therefore be justly looked upon as a punishment of their neglect to conquer other cities which God had given them that they were so long kept out of this. 3. Among the cities of Judah (in all 114) we meet with Libnah, which in Joram's days revolted, and probably set up for a free independent state (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.22">2 Kings viii. 22</reference>), and Lachish, where king Amaziah was slain (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.19">1 Kings xiv. 19</reference>); it led the dance in idolatry (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.13">Mic. i. 13</reference>); it was the <hi type="italic">beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion.</hi> Giloh, Ahithophel's town, is here mentioned, and Tekoa, of which the prophet Amos was, and near which Jehoshaphat obtained that glorious victory, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20-2Chr.20.30">2 Chron. xx. 20</reference>, &c., and Maresha, where Asa was a conqueror. Many of the cities of this tribe occur in the history of David's troubles. Adullam, Ziph, Keilah, Maon, Engedi, Ziklag, here reckoned in this tribe, were places near which David had most of his haunts; for, though sometimes Saul drove him out from the inheritance of the Lord, yet he kept as close to it as he could. The wilderness of Judah he frequented much, and in it John Baptist preached, and there the kingdom of heaven commenced, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Matt. iii. 1</reference>. The riches of this country no doubt answered Jacob's blessing of this tribe, that he should <hi type="italic">wash his garments in wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen. xlix. 11</reference>. And, in general, <hi type="italic">Judah, thou art he whom thy brethren shall praise,</hi> not envy.  <chapter eID="Josh.15"/> <div eID="gen4427" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb1e2aa6c721c6ab33a70a73866d9f6bea3240ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2118"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.15.1-Josh.15.12">Jos 15:1-12</reference>. Borders of the Lot of Judah.</title> <div sID="gen2845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2118"/><hi type="bold">1. This then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah--</hi>In what manner the lot was drawn on this occasion the sacred historian does not say; but it is probable that the method adopted was similar to that described in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.10">Jos 18:10</reference>. Though the general survey of the country had not been completed, some rough draft or delineation of the first conquered part must have been made, and satisfactory evidence obtained that it was large enough to furnish three cantons, before all the tribes cast lots for them; and they fell to Judah, Ephraim, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The lot of Judah came first, in token of the pre-eminence of that tribe over all the others; and its destined superiority thus received the visible sanction of God. The territory, assigned to it as a possession, was large and extensive, being bounded on the south by the wilderness of Zin, and the southern extremity of the Salt Sea (<reference osisRef="Num.34.3-Num.34.5">Nu 34:3-5</reference>); on the east, by that sea, extending to the point where it receives the waters of the Jordan; on the north, by a line drawn nearly parallel to Jerusalem, across the country, from the northern extremity of the Salt Sea to the southern limits of the Philistine territory, and to the Mediterranean; and on the west this sea was its boundary, as far as Sihor (Wady El-Arish). <div eID="gen2845" type="x-p"/>

He that smiteth Kirjath-sepher--</hi>This offer was made as an incentive to youthful bravery (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">1Sa 17:25</reference>); and the prize was won by Othniel, Caleb's younger brother (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.13">Jud 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>).
