entries.28f8379eab8e6d3813c2f9dfcb67bc998bd73938: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2129"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.63">Jos 15:21-63</reference>. Cities of Judah.</title> <div sID="gen2861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2129"/><hi type="bold">21-63. the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah--</hi>There is given a list of cities within the tribal territory of Judah, arranged in four divisions, corresponding to the districts of which it consisted--the cities in the southern part (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">Jos 15:21-32</reference>), those in the lowlands (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.33-Josh.15.47">Jos 15:33-47</reference>), those in the highlands (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.48-Josh.15.60">Jos 15:48-60</reference>), and those in the desert (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.61">Jos 15:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.62">62</reference>). One gets the best idea of the relative situation of these cities by looking at the map. <chapter eID="Josh.15"/>

entries.4cb0c07274557882b497e7765395056a74cea476: <div eID="gen7960" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7961" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7962" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7962" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7961" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7963" type="x-p"/> The lot of the tribe of Judah described, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.1">Jos 15:1</reference>. Their south border, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.2-Jos.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference>. Their east border, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.5-Jos.15.11">Jos 15:5-11</reference>. Their west border, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.12">Jos 15:12</reference>. Caleb's conquest, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.13-Jos.15.15">Jos 15:13-15</reference>. Promises his daughter to the person who should take Kirjath-sepher, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.16">Jos 15:16</reference>. Othniel his kinsman renders himself master of it, and gets Achsah to wife, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.17">Jos 15:17</reference>. Her request to her father to get a well watered land, which is granted, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.18">Jos 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.19">Jos 15:19</reference>. The cities of the tribe of Judah are enumerated, vv. 20-63. <div eID="gen7963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7964" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7965" type="x-p"/> This then was the lot of the tribe of - Judah - The geography of the sacred writings presents many difficulties, occasioned by the changes which the civil state of the promised land has undergone, especially for the last two thousand years. Many of the ancient towns and villages have had their names so totally changed, that their former appellations are no longer discernible; several lie buried under their own ruins, and others have been so long destroyed that not one vestige of them remains. On these accounts it is very difficult to ascertain the situation of many of the places mentioned in this and the following chapters. But however this may embarrass the commentator, it cannot affect the truth of the narrative. Some of the principal cities in the universe, cities that were the seats of the most powerful empires, are not only reduced to ruins, but so completely blotted out of the map of the world that their situation cannot be ascertained. Where is Babylon? Where are Nineveh, Carthage, Thebes, Tyre, Baalbec, Palmyra, and the so far-famed and greatly celebrated Troy? Of the former and the latter, so renowned by historians and poets, scarcely a vestige, properly speaking, remains; nor can the learned agree on the spot once occupied by the buildings of those celebrated cities! Should this circumstance invalidate the whole history of the ancient world, in which they made so conspicuous a figure? And can the authenticity of our sacred historian be impaired, because several of the places he mentions no longer exist? Surely no: nor can it be called in question but by the heedless and superficial, or the decidedly profane. Although some of the cities of the holy land are destroyed, and it would be difficult to ascertain the geography of several, yet enough remain, either under their ancient names, or with such decisive characteristics, that through their new names their ancient appellatives are readily discernible. It is natural to suppose that the division mentioned here was made after an accurate survey of the land, which might have been made by proper persons accompanying the conquering army of the Israelites. Nine tribes and a half were yet to be accommodated, and the land must be divided into nine parts and a half. This was no doubt done with the utmost judgment and discretion, the advantages and disadvantages of each division being carefully balanced. These were the portions which were divided by lot; and it appears that Judah drew the first lot; and, because of the importance and pre-eminence of this tribe, this lot is first described. <div eID="gen7965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> By their families - It is supposed that the family divisions were not determined by lot. These were left to the prudence and judgment of Joshua, Eleazar, and the ten princes, who appointed to each family a district in proportion to its number, etc., the general division being that alone which was determined by the lot. <div eID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7967" type="x-p"/> To the border of Edom - The tribe of Judah occupied the most southerly part of the land of Canaan. Its limits extended from the extremity of the Dead Sea southward, along Idumea, possibly by the desert of Sin, and proceeding from east to west to the Mediterranean Sea, and the most eastern branch of the river Nile, or to what is called the river of Egypt. Calmet very properly remarks, that Joshua is particular in giving the limits of this tribe, as being the first, the most numerous, most important; that which was to furnish the kings of Judea; that in which pure religion was to be preserved, and that from which the Messiah was to spring.
entries.66f1d022d96711ebfe4d60118947ef41b6c4cc3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> From the bay that looketh southward - These were the southern limits of the tribe of Judah, which commenced at the extremity of the lake Asphaltites or Dead Sea, and terminated at Sihor or the river of Egypt, and Mediterranean Sea; though some think it extended to the Nile.
entries.3720ebcd7356ef7180568c7fa9c65339c0d9f7c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> Maaleh-acrabbim - The ascent of the Mount of Scorpions, probably so called from the multitude of those animals found in that place. <div eID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> Kadesh-barnea - This place was called Enmishpat, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Gen 14:7</reference>. It was on the edge of the wilderness of Paran, and about twenty-four miles from Hebron. Here Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, died; and here Moses and Aaron rebelled against the Lord; hence the place was called Meribah-Kadesh, or the contention of Kadesh. <div eID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> Karkaa - Supposed to be the Coracea of Ptolemy, in Arabia Petraea. - Calmet.
entries.adf00b6dcabb4cf91480dc20e99aa90e8ec72610: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> Toward Azmon - This was the last city they possessed toward Egypt. <div eID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7973" type="x-p"/> The river of Egypt - The most eastern branch of the river Nile. See on <reference osisRef="Jos.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference> (note). But there is much reason to doubt whether any branch of the Nile be meant, and whether the promised land extended to that river. On this subject it is impossible to decide either way.
entries.7bfc2b36cc1cd9bf811067d1b9891fcde0dcf2fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7974" type="x-p"/> The east border was the Salt Sea - The Salt Sea is the same as the Dead Sea, lake Asphaltites, etc. And here it is intimated that the eastern border of the tribe of Judah extended along the Dead Sea, from its lowest extremity to the end of Jordan, i.e., to the place where Jordan falls into this sea.
entries.02a371a994a5725fd285395ad50ca0be39ed662b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7975" type="x-p"/> Beth-hogla - A place between Jericho and the Dead Sea, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.21">Jos 18:21</reference>, though here serving as a frontier to the tribe of Judah. <div eID="gen7975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7976" type="x-p"/> Stone of Bohan - This must have been some remarkable place, probably like the stone of Jacob, which afterwards became Bethel; but where it was situated is uncertain.
entries.ad83ef585c93930e871edde46bdaa9a27b702820: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> The valley of Achor - Debir mentioned in this verse is unknown. The valley of Achor had its name from the punishment of Achan. See the account, <reference osisRef="Jos.7.24">Jos 7:24</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> En-shemesh - The fountain of the sun; it was eastward of Jerusalem, on the confines of Judah and Benjamin.
entries.93d3f1a9f92208fce8b384c9f0cd3646c10d363f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> The valley of the son of Hinnom - Who Hinnom was is not known, nor why this was called his valley. It was situated on the east of Jerusalem; and is often mentioned in Scripture. The image of the idol Molech appears to have been set up there; and there the idolatrous Israelites caused their sons and daughters to pass through the fire in honor of that demon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Kgs 23:10</reference>. It was also called Tophet, see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">Jer 7:32</reference>. When King Josiah removed the image of this idol from this valley, it appears to have been held in such universal execration, that it became the general receptacle of all the filth and impurities which were carried out of Jerusalem; and it is supposed that continual fires were there kept up, to consume those impurities and prevent infection. From the Hebrew words גי בן הנם gei ben Hinnom, the valley of the son of Hinnom, and by contraction, גי הנם gei Hinnom, the valley of Hinnom, came the Γεεννα, Gehenna of the New Testament, called also Γεεννα του πυρος, the Gehenna of fire, which is the emblem of hell, or the place of the damned. See <reference osisRef="Mat.5.22">Mat 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.5.29">Mat 5:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.5.30">Mat 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.28">Mat 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.18.9">Mat 18:9</reference>, etc. In the East it is common to add the name of the father to that of the son, e.g., "This land belongs to Goborka the son of Kake Prusada." But this addition is not made till after the father's death. This custom prevailed also in the west. It is common among the aborigines of both Ireland and Wales. <div eID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> The same is Jerusalem - This city was formerly called Jebus; a part of it was in the tribe of Benjamin; Zion, called its citadel, was in the tribe of Judah. <div eID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> The valley of the giants - Of the Rephaim. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Gen 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.2.7">Deu 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.11">Deu 2:11</reference>. On this subject, a very intelligent clergyman favors me with his opinion in the following terms: - "The boundary between Judah and Benjamin went up from the valley of Hinnom on the east to the top of the hill southward, leaving Jebusi (or Jerusalem) to the northwest adjoining to Benjamin. This mount (Jebusi) lay between the two tribes, which the Jebusites possessed till the time of David. At the 63d verse here, it is said Judah could not drive out these people; and in <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.21">Jdg 1:21</reference>, the same is said of the Benjamites. Each tribe might have attacked them at various times. There were various mounts or tops to these hills. Mount Zion and Moriah, where the temple stood, was in the tribe of Judah; <reference osisRef="Psa.78.68">Psa 78:68</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.69">Psa 78:69</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.87.2">Psa 87:2</reference>. "In <reference osisRef="Deu.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference> it is said of Benjamin, the Lord shall dwell by him, i.e., near him, or beside his borders, between his shoulders; the line might be circular between the two hills or tops so as in part to encompass Mount Zion in the tribe of Judah, on which the temple stood. Benjamin's gate, (mentioned <reference osisRef="Jer.37.12">Jer 37:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jer 37:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.7">Jer 38:7</reference>), was the gate leading out of the city, into the tribe of Benjamin. So the gate of Ephraim, (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.13">2Kgs 14:13</reference>), was a gate which led towards the tribe of Ephraim. We give names to roads, etc., in the same way now. "Mount Calvary, (which was on the outside of the gate), seems to have been in the tribe of Benjamin. Query. Whether Calvary or Golgotha was so called from skulls being scattered about there, (as say some), or rather from the figure of the rock being shaped like a man's skull, with one face of it nearly perpendicular? I incline to this latter opinion. I believe the Jews did not suffer human bones, even of malefactors, to lie about." - J. C.
entries.ca7bc56302d307510e10ac655d13e9f63c696019: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> Baalah, which is Kirjath-jearim - This place was rendered famous in Scripture, in consequence of its being the residence of the ark, for twenty years after it was sent back by the Philistines; see 1 Samuel 5:1-7:2.
entries.b94b7274c0ed7d4d6ced7bd7f4358ed2f292922e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> Beth-shemesh - The house or temple of the sun. It is evident that the sun was an object of adoration among the Canaanites; and hence fountains, hills, etc., were dedicated to him. Beth-shemesh is remarkable for the slaughter of its inhabitants, in consequence of their prying curiously, if not impiously, into the ark of the Lord, when sent back by the Philistines. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.19">1Sam 6:19</reference>.
entries.58416df7795692279dd831b21ebe9222175fb399: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> The great sea - The Mediterranean.
entries.d460a241c3d7a6a3a5206c23ebea332f1985951a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> And unto Caleb - he gave a part - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Jos.14.14">Jos 14:14</reference>, etc.
entries.5015188feb6113cecba9725be29cc93c55c2cfd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7986" type="x-p"/> The three sons of Anak - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.14.15">Jos 14:15</reference> (note).
entries.4c0ae777dc3556a3da87f2d53930255e3727c041: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen7986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7987" type="x-p"/> Kirjath-sepher - The city of the book. Why so named is uncertain. It was also called Debir, and Kirjath-sannah. See <reference osisRef="Jos.15.49">Jos 15:49</reference>.
entries.967d30da749e6c0bf62d21a0dcee69d5a0fe1934: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen7987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> Will I give Achsah my daughter - In ancient times fathers assumed an absolute right over their children, especially in disposing of them in marriage; and it was customary for a king or great man to promise his daughter in marriage to him who should take a city, kill an enemy, etc. So Saul promised his daughter in marriage to him who should kill Goliath, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">1Sam 17:25</reference>; and Caleb offers his on this occasion to him who should take Kirjath-sepher. Profane writers furnish many similar examples.
entries.e716ff310f4a2c2cc4467e718e2e2645be153b61: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> As she came - As she was now departing from the house of her father to go to that of her husband. <div eID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> She moved him - Othniel, to ask of her father a field, one on which she had set her heart, as contiguous to the patrimony already granted. <div eID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7991" type="x-p"/> She lighted off her ass - ותצנח vattitsnach, she hastily, suddenly alighted, as if she had forgotten something, or was about to return to her father's house. Which being perceived by her father, he said, What wouldest thou? What is the matter? What dost thou want?
entries.7bf99129e4e2b827e4fa15433c0c7672c9b518ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen7991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7992" type="x-p"/> Give me a blessing - Do me an act of kindness. Grant me a particular request. <div eID="gen7992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> Thou hast given me a south land - Which was probably dry, or very ill, watered. <div eID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> Give me also springs of water - Let me have some fields in which there are brooks or wells already digged. <div eID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> The upper springs, and the nether springs - He gave her even more than she requested; he gave her a district among the mountains and another in the plains well situated and well watered. There are several difficulties in this account, with which I shall not trouble the reader. What is mentioned above appears to be the sense.
entries.55326e085d75ca08621b815697755709aece564a: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> Ziph - There were two cities of this name in the tribe of Judah, that mentioned here, and another <reference osisRef="Jos.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>. One of these two is noted for the refuge of David when persecuted by Saul; and the attempts made by its inhabitants to deliver him into the hands of his persecutor. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14-1Sam.23.24">1Sam 23:14-24</reference>.
entries.6735f7b41ecd6591377f2c0ab29e8ac5e009bbc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> Beer-sheba - A city, famous in the book of Genesis as the residence of the patriarchs Abraham and Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.19">Gen 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.10">Gen 28:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1">Gen 46:1</reference>. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.21.31">Gen 21:31</reference>. It lay on the way between Canaan and Egypt, about forty miles from Jerusalem.
entries.78294b27869787682621b2fbbeece3d18c64764d: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> Hormah - A place rendered famous by the defeat of the Hebrews by the Canaanites. See <reference osisRef="Num.14.45">Num 14:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.44">Deu 1:44</reference>.
entries.817688bbdc426bf327ecd042999aa73d91ad73c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7999" type="x-p"/> Ziklag - The Philistines seem to have kept possession of this city till the time of David, who received it from Achish, king of Gath, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sam 27:6</reference>; after which time it remained in the possession of the kings of Judah.
entries.8180f720962daac9933cea8a6eff9fb475f06b01: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen7999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8000" type="x-p"/> All the cities are twenty and nine, with their villages - But on a careful examination we shall find thirty-eight; but it is supposed that nine of these are excepted; viz., Beersheba, Moladah, Hazarshual, Baalah, Azem, Hormah, Ziklag, Ain, and Rimmon, which were afterwards given to the tribe of Simeon. This may appear satisfactory, but perhaps the truth will be found to be this: Several cities in the promised land are expressed by compound terms; not knowing the places, different translations combine what should be separated, and in many cases separate what should be combined. Through this we have cities formed out of epithets. On this ground we have thirty-eight cities as the sum here, instead of twenty-nine.
entries.d50e40cd782287ccd0038ecc2d5533bd56bb2146: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen8000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> Eshtaol, and Zoreah - Here Samson was buried, it being the burial-place of his fathers; see <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.31">Jdg 16:31</reference>. These places though first given to Judah, afterwards fell to the lot of Dan, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.41">Jos 19:41</reference>.
entries.eeec50d84b30568dcf43d216abbd30cecd7eebdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> Jarmuth - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference>. <div eID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> Adullam - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.15">Jos 12:15</reference>. <div eID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> Socoh - It was near this place that David fought with and slew Goliath, the champion of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1">1Sam 17:1</reference>.
entries.f311c0a9da041f0a1bcb02dd88430a3d316db022: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8005" type="x-p"/> Gederah - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.13">Jos 12:13</reference>. <div eID="gen8005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8006" type="x-p"/> Fourteen cities - Well reckoned, we shall find fifteen cities here; but probably Gederah and Gederothaim (<reference osisRef="Jos.15.36">Jos 15:36</reference>) are the same. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.32">Jos 15:32</reference>.
entries.ea02068b06cfff1266ffddfb7b078f2db8d2d556: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen8006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8007" type="x-p"/> Lachish - and Eglon - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference> (note).
entries.949fd9ede4f1beea5f7b10f29b8c594dac607694: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen8007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8008" type="x-p"/> Beth-dagon - The house or temple of Dagon. This is a well known idol of the Philistines, and probably the place mentioned here was in some part of their territories; but the situation at present is unknown.
entries.2cf96257e61758adb1847b2a24d0ff794d7b7e57: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen8008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8009" type="x-p"/> Libnah - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.10.29">Jos 10:29</reference>. <div eID="gen8009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8010" type="x-p"/> Ether - From <reference osisRef="Jos.19.7">Jos 19:7</reference> we learn that this city was afterwards given to the tribe of Simeon.
entries.ceca75b473aa80f6c013b6792891ab34ec199f04: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen8010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8011" type="x-p"/> Keilah - This town was near Hebron, and is said to have been the burying-place of the prophet Habakkuk. David obliged the Philistines to raise the siege of it; (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1-1Sam.23.13">1Sam 23:1-13</reference>); but finding that its inhabitants had purposed to deliver him into the hands of Saul, who was coming in pursuit of him, he made his escape. See this remarkable case explained in the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference> (note). <div eID="gen8011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8012" type="x-p"/> Mareshah - Called also Maresheth and Marasthi; it was the birth-place of the prophet Micah. Near this place was the famous battle between Asa, king of Judah, and Zera, king of Cush or Ethiopia, who was at the head of one thousand thousand men, and three hundred chariots. Asa defeated this immense host and took much spoil, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9-2Chr.14.15">2Chr 14:9-15</reference>.
entries.11dfc1df57f76794e61ee9730a61aae384ac9917: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen8012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8013" type="x-p"/> Ekron - One of the five Philistine lordships; see the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>.
entries.b7dcd5ec49552e8e9595b61baa99db5db8a039cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen8013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8014" type="x-p"/> Ashdod - Called also Azotus, <reference osisRef="Act.8.40">Act 8:40</reference>. <div eID="gen8014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8015" type="x-p"/> Unto the river of Egypt - The Pelusiac branch of the Nile, or Sihor. But see on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.4">Jos 15:4</reference> (note). <div eID="gen8015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8016" type="x-p"/> The great sea - The Mediterranean.
entries.4e7b7fd7071479870514bc64d98a23d1d91239f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen8016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8017" type="x-p"/> Socoh - See a town of this name, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference> (note).
entries.4780814b04195ecaf8b635cf5bd9d0c5d91895ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen8017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8018" type="x-p"/> Kirjath-sannah - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.15">Jos 15:15</reference>.
entries.d9e86c75f7cd496d1ac907e95254baa17285b72e: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen8018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8019" type="x-p"/> Goshen - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.10.41">Jos 10:41</reference>. <div eID="gen8019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8020" type="x-p"/> Giloh - The country of the traitor Ahithophel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.12">2Sam 15:12</reference>.
entries.1aa5906ce9e581c15022b6ff54a91d702f3a37e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 53</hi> <div eID="gen8020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8021" type="x-p"/> Beth-tappuah - The house of the apple or citron tree. Probably a place where these grew in great abundance and perfection. <div eID="gen8021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8022" type="x-p"/> Aphekah - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.18">Jos 12:18</reference>.
entries.eb61b5c2f876b12a63c1456b693a1f38c701d91e: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen8022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8023" type="x-p"/> Kirjath-arba - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.14.15">Jos 14:15</reference>.
entries.7c10ec0d2e76c288e6ce34b9c9e60ada2f2c1601: <hi type="bold">Verse 55</hi> <div eID="gen8023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8024" type="x-p"/> Maon - In a desert to which this town gave name, David took refuge for a considerable time from the persecution of Saul; and in this place Nabal the Carmelite had great possessions. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.24">1Sam 23:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.25">1Sam 23:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2">1Sam 25:2</reference>. <div eID="gen8024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8025" type="x-p"/> Carmel - Not the celebrated mount of that name, but a village, the residence of Nabal. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2">1Sam 25:2</reference>. It was near Maon, mentioned above, and was about ten miles eastward of Hebron. It is the place where Saul erected a trophy to himself after the defeat of the Amalekites; see <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12">1Sam 15:12</reference>. <div eID="gen8025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8026" type="x-p"/> Ziph - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.24">Jos 15:24</reference> (note).
entries.384397898bf461d3e5cee144281c6632d2655241: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen8026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8027" type="x-p"/> Timnah - A frontier town of the Philistines; it was in this place that Samson got his wife, see Judges 14:1-15:20.
entries.0818f6a31ac50ee3c77e88fa715dc2530aba4624: <hi type="bold">Verse 58</hi> <div eID="gen8027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8028" type="x-p"/> Gedor - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.13">Jos 12:13</reference>. In this place the Alexandrian MS. of the Septuagint and the Codex Vaticanus add the eleven following towns: Theca, and Ephratha, (that is, Bethlehem), and Phagor, and Etan, and Kulon, and Tatam, and Thebes, and Karam, and Galam, and Thether, and Manocho; eleven cities and their villages. St. Jerome, on <reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic 5:1</reference>, mentions them, so that we find they were in the copies he used. Dr. Kennicott contends that they should be restored to the text, and accounts thus for their omission: "The same word וחצרויהן vechatsreyhen, and their villages, occurring immediately before this passage and at the end of it, the transcriber's eye passed from one to the other by mistake. A similar accident has caused the omission of two whole verses, the 35th and 36th of Joshua 21." See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.21.35">Jos 21:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.36">Jos 21:36</reference>.
entries.c9970f8719b5fb0b1bb507dbf34a8cca880a9893: <hi type="bold">Verse 60</hi> <div eID="gen8028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8029" type="x-p"/> Kirjath-baal - The same as Baalah. See on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.9">Jos 15:9</reference> (note).
entries.5c7ff72af99607886ac129147acbcda8d6d54b42: <hi type="bold">Verse 62</hi> <div eID="gen8029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8030" type="x-p"/> The city of Salt - Or of Melach. This city was somewhere in the vicinity of the lake Asphaltites, the waters of which are the saltest perhaps in the world. The whole country abounds with salt: see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.19.25">Gen 19:25</reference>. Some suppose that it is the same as Zoar, the place to which Lot escaped after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. <div eID="gen8030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8031" type="x-p"/> En-gedi - The well of the kid: it was situated between Jericho and the lake of Sodom or Dead Sea.
entries.332b7b15e13c74af792758798d5dddf40821fa71: <hi type="bold">Verse 63</hi> <div eID="gen8031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8032" type="x-p"/> The Jebusites dwell - at Jerusalem unto this day - The whole history of Jerusalem, previously to the time of David, is encumbered with many difficulties. Sometimes it is attributed to Judah, sometimes to Benjamin, and it is probable that, being on the frontiers of both those tribes, each possessed a part of it. If the Jebusites were ever driven out before the time of David, it is certain they recovered it again, or at least a part of it - what is called the citadel or strong hold of Zion, (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7">2Sam 5:7</reference>), which he took from them; after which the city fell wholly into the hands of the Israelites. This verse is an additional proof that the book of Joshua was not written after the times of the Jewish kings, as some have endeavored to prove; for when this verse was written, the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Judah, which they did not after the days of David; therefore the book was written before there were any kings in Judea. <div eID="gen8032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8033" type="x-p"/> It is very likely, not only that many cities have by the lapse of time changed their names or been totally destroyed, (see the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.1">Jos 15:1</reference>), but that the names of those in the preceding catalogue have been changed also, several of them repeated that should have been mentioned but once, and not a few confounded with the terms by which they are described. But we must not suppose that every repetition of the name is through the carelessness of copyists; for there are often two places which bear the same name, which is frequently the case in England. But besides this, villages are mentioned as being apparently in the tribe of Judah, which afterwards appear to have been in an other tribe. The reason appears to be this: many towns are mentioned which were frontier towns, and when the limits of a tribe are pointed out, such places must necessarily be mentioned, though allotted to a different tribe. This consideration will serve to remove several difficulties which occur in the reading of this and the following chapters.  <chapter eID="Josh.15"/> <div eID="gen8033" type="x-p"/>

entries.755281123e564739cec874b9b95c7bad4b693d9b: <div eID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Inheritance of the Tribe of Judah - Joshua 15</title> <div sID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> Under the superintending providence of God, the inheritance which fell to the tribe of Judah by lot was in the southern part of Canaan, where Caleb had already received his inheritance, so that he was not separated from his tribe. The inheritance of Judah is first of all described according to its boundaries (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.1-Josh.15.12">Jos 15:1-12</reference>); then for the sake of completeness it is stated once more with regard to Caleb, that he received Kirjath-arba for his inheritance, and took possession of it by expelling the Anakites and conquering Debir (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.13-Josh.15.20">Jos 15:13-20</reference>); and after this a list is given of the towns in the different parts (vv. 21-63).<hi type="italic">Boundaries of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah</hi>. - Jos 15:1. Its situation in the land. “<hi type="italic">And there was</hi> (i.e., fell, or came out; cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1">Jos 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.1">Jos 19:1</reference>)<hi type="italic">the lot to the tribe of Judah according to its families to the frontier of Edom</hi> (see at Num 34:3), <hi type="italic">to the desert of Zin southward, against the extreme south</hi>” (lit. from the end or extremity of the south), i.e., its inheritance fell to it, so that it reached to the territory of Edom and the desert of Zin, in which Kadesh was situated (see at Num 13:21), on the extreme south of Canaan.
entries.87a9f0ed69b0c949961f901eef73fe37cdf15851: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.2-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference> <hi type="italic">The southern boundary</hi>. This was also the southern boundary of the land of Israel generally, and coincided with the southern boundary of Canaan as described in Num 34:3-5. It went out “<hi type="italic">from the end of the salt sea, namely, from the tongue which turneth to the south</hi>,” i.e., from the southern point of the Dead Sea, which is now a salt marsh.
entries.d8db860f940a362eff33a05a740265a7d2675720: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5">Jos 15:5</reference> “The eastern boundary was the salt sea to the end of the Jordan,” i.e., the Dead Sea, in all its length up to the point where the Jordan entered it.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.11">Jos 15:5-11</reference> <div eID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.11">Jos 15:5-11</reference> we have a description of the <hi type="italic">northern</hi> boundary, which is repeated in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.15-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:15-19</reference> as the southern boundary of Benjamin, though in the opposite direction, namely, from west to east. It started “<hi type="italic">from the tongue of the (salt) sea, the end (i.e., the mouth) of the Jordan, and went up to Beth-hagla</hi>,” - a border town between Judah and Benjamin, which was afterwards allotted to the latter (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.19">Jos 18:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.12">Jos 18:12</reference>), the present Ain Hajla, an hour and a quarter to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Riha</hi> (Jericho), and three-quarters of an hour from the Jordan (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.50.11">Gen 50:11</reference>, note), - “<hi type="italic">and went over to the north side of Beth-arabah</hi>,” a town in the desert of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.61">Jos 15:61</reference>), afterwards assigned to Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>), and called <hi type="italic">Ha-arabah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.18">Jos 18:18</reference>, about twenty or thirty minutes to the south-west of <hi type="italic">Ain Hajla</hi>, in a “level and barren steppe” (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, R. ii. p. 302), with which the name very well agrees (see also <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. pp. 268ff.). “<hi type="italic">And the border went up to the stone of Bohan, the son of Reuben</hi>.” The expression “went up” shows that the stone of <hi type="italic">Bohan</hi> must have been on higher ground, i.e., near the western mountains, though the opposite expression “went down” in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.17">Jos 18:17</reference> shows that it must have been by the side of the mountain, and not upon the top. According to <reference osisRef="Josh.18.18-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:18-19</reference>, the border went over from the stone of Bohan in an easterly direction “<hi type="italic">to the shoulder over against (Beth) Arabah northwards, and went down to </hi>(Beth)<hi type="italic">Arabah, and then went over to the shoulder of Beth-hagla northwards</hi>,” i.e., on the north side of the mountain ridge of Beth-arabah and Beth-hagla. This ridge is “the chain of hills or downs which runs from <hi type="italic">Kasr Hajla</hi> towards the south to the north side of the Dead Sea, and is called <hi type="italic">Katar Hhadije</hi>, i.e., a row of camels harnessed together.”
entries.e169654219878b9387ff4bd58504efb1d0aed037: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.13-Josh.15.19">Jos 15:13-19</reference> <div eID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> The account of the conquest of the inheritance, which Caleb asked for and received before the lots were cast for the land (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.6-Josh.14.15">Jos 14:6-15</reference>), by the extermination of the Anakites from Hebron, and the capture of the fortified town of Debir, is repeated with very slight differences in Jdg 1:10-15, in the enumeration of the different conflicts in which the separate tribes engaged after the death of Joshua, in order to secure actual possession of the inheritance which had fallen to them by lot, and is neither copied from our book by the author of the book of Judges, nor taken from Judges by the author of Joshua; but both of them have drawn it from one common source, upon which the accounts of the conquest of Canaan contained in the book of Joshua are generally founded.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.13">Jos 15:13</reference> <div eID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> As an introduction to the account of the conquest of Hebron and Debir, the fact that they gave Caleb his portion among the sons of Judah, namely Hebron, is first of all repeated from Jos 14:13. נתן impers., they gave, i.e., Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.13">Jos 14:13</reference>). The words “<hi type="italic">according to the command of Jehovah to Joshua</hi>” are to be explained from <reference osisRef="Josh.14.9-Josh.14.12">Jos 14:9-12</reference>, according to which Jehovah had promised, in the hearing of Joshua, to give Caleb possession of the mountains of Hebron, even when they were at Kadesh (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.12">Jos 14:12</reference>). The “father of Anak” is the tribe father of the family of Anakites in Hebron, from whom this town received the name of <hi type="italic">Kirjath-arba</hi>; see at Num 13:22 and Gen 23:2.
entries.a2ff56792f049961bdc211ed040842abbf9ae5e0: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">Jos 15:21-32</reference> <div eID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2881" type="x-p"/> The towns in the <hi type="italic">south land</hi>. - <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> (south-land) was the name given to the southernmost district of Canaan in its full extent, from the Arabah, at the southern end of the Dead Sea, right across to the coast of the Mediterranean, and from the southern border of Canaan, as described in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.2-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference>, as far north as Wady <hi type="italic">Sheriah</hi>, below Gaza, on the western side, and up to the mountains and desert of Judah on the east, stretching across the wadys of <hi type="italic">es Seba, Milh,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ehdeib</hi>, above which that part of Palestine commences where rain is more abundant, and to which, as we have already observed at Num 13:17, the <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> formed a kind of intermediate link between the fertile land and the desert. It was a line of steppe-land, with certain patches here and there that admitted of cultivation, but in which tracts of heath prevailed, for the most part covered with grass and bushes, where only grazing could be carried on with any success. The term which <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> employ for <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> is <hi type="italic">Daromas</hi>, but they carry it farther northwards than the Negeb of the Old Testament (see <hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, Pal. Ill. pp. 185ff). The numerous towns mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">Jos 15:21-32</reference> as standing in the <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi>, may none of them have been large or of any importance. In the list before us we find that, as a rule, several names are closely connected together by the copula vav, and in this way the whole may be divided into four separate groups of towns.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.23">Jos 15:21-23</reference> <hi type="italic">First</hi> group of nine places. - Jos 15:21. The towns “<hi type="italic">from</hi>,” i.e., at “<hi type="italic">the end of the tribe-territory of Judah, towards the territory of Edom</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Kabzeel</hi>: the home of the hero Benaiah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>), probably identical with <hi type="italic">Jakabzeel</hi>, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.25">Neh 11:25</reference> in connection with <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, but has not been discovered. This also applies to <hi type="italic">Eder</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jagur</hi>.
entries.5d2a08198a273c7be01a9d7967505d8504274975: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33-Josh.15.47">Jos 15:33-47</reference> <div eID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> Towns in the <hi type="italic">lowland</hi> or <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>. - The lowland (<hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>), which is generally rendered ἡ πεδινή in the <hi type="italic">Sept.</hi>, rarely τὸ πεδιόν (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.7">Deu 1:7</reference>), but which is transferred as a proper name ἡ Σεφηλά in Oba 1:19; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jer 32:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.13">Jer 33:13</reference>, as well as in 1 Macc. 12:38, where even <hi type="italic">Luther</hi> has <hi type="italic">Sephela</hi>, is the name given to the land between the mountains of Judah and the Mediterranean Sea, - a broad plain of undulating appearance, intersected by heights and low ranges of hills, with fertile soil, in which corn fields alternate with meadows, gardens, and extensive olive groves. It is still tolerably well cultivated, and is covered with villages, which are situated for the most part upon the different hills. Towards the south, the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> was bounded by the Negeb  (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>); on the north, it reached to Ramleh and Lydda, or Diospolis, where the plain of Sharon began, - a plain which extended as far as Carmel, and was renowned for the beauty of its flowers. Towards the east the hills multiply and shape themselves into a hilly landscape, which forms the intermediate link between the mountains and the plain, and which is distinguished from the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> itself, in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">Jos 10:40</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.8">Jos 12:8</reference>, under the name of <hi type="italic">Ashedoth</hi>, or <hi type="italic">slopes</hi>, whereas here it is reckoned as forming part of the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>. This hilly tract is more thickly studded with villages than even the actual plain (See <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 363, and iii. p. 29.) The towns in the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> are divided into four groups.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33-Josh.15.36">Jos 15:33-36</reference> <div eID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2884" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">first</hi> group contains the towns in the northern part of the hilly region or slopes, which are reckoned as forming part of the lowland: in all, fourteen towns. The most northerly part of this district was given up to the tribe of Dan on the second division (Jos 19:41.). <hi type="italic">Eshtaol</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zoreah</hi>, which were assigned to the tribe of Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.41">Jos 19:41</reference>), and were partly inhabited by Danites (Jdg 13:25; Jdg 18:2, Jdg 18:8,Jdg 18:11) and partly by families of Judah, who had gone out from Kirjath-jearim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.53">1Ch 1:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.2">1Ch 4:2</reference>), probably after the removal of the 600 Danites to Laish-Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.47">Jos 19:47</reference>; Jdg 18:1), were situated, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Esthaul</hi> and <hi type="italic">Saara</hi>), ten Roman miles to the north of Eleutheropolis, on the road to Nicopolis. <hi type="italic">Zoreah</hi>, the home of Samson, who was buried between Zoreah and Eshtaol (Jdg 13:2; Jdg 16:31), was fortified by Rehoboam, and still inhabited by Judaeans after the captivity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.10">2Ch 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.29">Neh 11:29</reference>); it has been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Surá</hi>, at the south-western end of the mountain range which bounds the Wady es Surar on the north (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 341, and Bibl. Res. p. 153). <hi type="italic">Eshtaol</hi> has probably been preserved in <hi type="italic">Um Eshteiyeh</hi>, to the south-west (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 342). <hi type="italic">Ashnah</hi> is possibly to be read <hi type="italic">Ashvah</hi>, according to the lxx, Cod. Vat. (Ἄσσα). In that case it might resemble a town on the east of Zorea (<hi type="italic">Tobler</hi>, p. 180), as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes.
entries.c9b98f08b99894729f649818a6ad96361a5a815f: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.48-Josh.15.60">Jos 15:48-60</reference> <div eID="gen2888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2889" type="x-p"/> The towns on the <hi type="italic">mountains</hi> are divided into five, or more correctly, into six groups. The mountains of Judah, which rise precipitously from the Negeb, between the hilly district on the west, which is reckoned as part of the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>, and the desert of Judah, extending to the Dead Sea on the east (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.61">Jos 15:61</reference>), attain the height of 3000 feet above the level of the sea, in the neighbourhood of Hebron, and run northwards to the broad wady of Beit-hanina, above Jerusalem. They are a large rugged range of limestone mountains, with many barren and naked peaks, whilst the sides are for the most part covered with grass, shrubs, bushes, and trees, and the whole range is intersected by many very fruitful valleys. <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> describes it as abounding in corn, fruit, and wine; and to the present day it contains many orchards, olive grounds, and vineyards, rising in terraces up the sides of the mountains, whilst the valleys and lower grounds yield plentiful harvests of wheat, millet, and other kinds of corn. In ancient times, therefore, the whole of this district was thickly covered with towns (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. pp. 185, 191-2, and <hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 45ff.).  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.48-Josh.15.51">Jos 15:48-51</reference> <div eID="gen2889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2890" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">first</hi> group consists of eleven towns on the south-west of the mountains.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.48">Jos 15:48</reference> <hi type="italic">Shamir</hi> has probably been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Um Shaumerah</hi>, mentioned by <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (iii. App.), though the situation of these ruins has not yet been precisely determined. <hi type="italic">Jattir</hi>, which was given up to the priests (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.14">Jos 21:14</reference>), and is mentioned again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.27">1Sa 30:27</reference>, is described in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Jether</hi>) as a large placed inhabited by Christians, twenty miles from Eleutheropolis, <hi type="italic">in interiori Daroma juxta Malathan</hi>, - a description which suits the ruins of <hi type="italic">Attir</hi>, in the southern portion of the mountains (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 194; called <hi type="italic">Ater</hi> by <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, R. iii. p. 6). <hi type="italic">Socoh</hi>, two hours N.W. of this, the present <hi type="italic">Shuweikeh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 194), called <hi type="italic">Suêche</hi> by <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> (R. iii. p. 29), a village about four hours from Hebron.
entries.cf320178772a8080fbfd23d75f78541290c6bce7: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.61-Josh.15.62">Jos 15:61-62</reference> <div eID="gen2895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">towns in the desert of Judah</hi>, which ran along the Dead Sea from the northern border of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">Jos 15:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.7">Jos 15:7</reference>) to Wady Fikreh on the south, and reached to the districts of Maon, Ziph, Tekoah, and Bethlehem towards the west. This tract of land is for the most part a terrible desert, with a soil composed of chalk, marl, and limestone, and with bald mountains covered with flint and hornstone, and without the slightest trace of vegetation on the side bordering on the Dead Sea (see <hi type="italic">v. Schubert</hi>, Reise, iii. pp. 94, 96; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. pp. 202, 475, 477). Yet wherever there are springs even this desert is covered with a luxuriant vegetation, as far as the influence of the water extends (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. pp. 249, 258); and even in those parts which are now completely desolate, there are traces of the work of man of a very ancient date in all directions (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 187). Six towns are mentioned in the verses before us. <hi type="italic">Beth-arabah:</hi> see at Jos 15:6. <hi type="italic">Middin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Secaca</hi> are unknown. According to <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, <hi type="italic">Middin</hi> is probably the ruins of <hi type="italic">Mird</hi> or <hi type="italic">Mardeh</hi>, to the west of the northern end of the Dead Sea (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 270).
entries.82258a221dedd81e4da18cf061bd819b85e741a7: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference> <div eID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2897" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference> there follows a notice to the effect that the Judaeans were unable to expel the Jebusites from Jerusalem, which points back to the time immediately after Joshua, when the Judaeans had taken Jerusalem and burned it (Jdg 1:8), but were still unable to maintain possession. This notice is not at variance with either <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference> or Jdg 1:21, since it neither affirms that Jerusalem belonged to the tribe of Judah, nor that Judah alone laid claim to the possession of the town to the exclusion of the Benjamites (see the explanation of Jdg 1:8).  <chapter eID="Josh.15"/> <div eID="gen2897" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a202851f3cc8fe36eff251fd5d52f2b9f6a50f1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.15.1" sID="gen23881" type="section"/> <div sID="gen23882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> I have already premised, that I would not be very exact in delineating the site of places, and in discussing names, partly because I admit that I am not well acquainted with topographical or chorographic science, and partly because great labor would produce little fruit to the reader; <note n="144"> <div sID="gen23883" type="x-p"/> French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Jai desia par ci devant adverti que je ne seroye point curieux a desrire ou peindre la situation des lieux, et a espulcher tous les noms, en partie parce que je confesse franchement que je ne suis pas bien exerce a faire descriptions de lieux ou de regions; en partie d’autant que d’un grand travail qu’il faudroit prendre, il n’en reviendroit que bien peu de fruict aux lecteurs</foreign>;” “I have already before this intimated that I would not be curious in describing or painting the situation of places, and in expiscating all the names, partly because, I frankly confess, that I am not much experienced in making descriptions of places or countries, partly because from the great labor which it would be necessary to take, very little benefit would redound to the reader.” It may be added that these descriptions of boundaries, how minutely soever they may be detailed, must, from their very nature, leave a very vague impression on the mind of the most careful reader, and are much less adapted for the ear than for the eye, which, by a single glance at a map, furnishes information much more vivid, distinct, and accurate than can be obtained from pages of description. At the same time it ought to be remembered, that accurate and detailed descriptions of the boundaries of the different tribes were absolutely indispensable to the Israelites themselves, to whom they formed a kind of title-deeds, vindicating their right of possession, and securing them against encroachment. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen23883" type="x-p"/> </note> nay, perhaps the greater part of readers would toil and perplex themselves without receiving any benefit. With regard to the subject in hand, it is to be observed, that the lot of the tribe of Judah not only falls on elevated ground, the very elevation of the territory, indicating the dignity of the future kingdom, but a similar presage is given by its being the first lot that turns up. What had already been obtained by arms, they begin to divide. The names of the ten tribes are cast into the urn. Judah is preferred to all the others. Who does not see that it is raised to the highest rank, in order that the prophecy of Jacob may be fulfilled? Then within the limits here laid down, it is well known that there were rich pastures, and vineyards celebrated for their productiveness and the excellence of their wines. In this way, while the lot corresponds with the prophecy of Jacob, it is perfectly clear that it did not so happen by chance; the holy patriarch had only uttered what was dictated by the Spirit.<div eID="gen23882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23884" type="x-p"/>If any are better skilled in places, a more minute investigation will be pleasant and useful to them. But lest those who are less informed feel it irksome to read unknown names, let them consider that they have obtained knowledge of no small value, provided they bear in mind the facts to which I have briefly and summarily adverted — that the tribe of Judah was placed on elevated ground, that it might be more conspicuous than the others, until the scepter should arise from it — and that a region of fruitful vineyards and rich pastures was assigned to his posterity — and, finally, all this was done, in order that the whole people might recognize that there was nothing of the nature of chance in the turning up of a lot, which had been foretold three centuries before. Besides, it is easy for the unlearned to infer from the long circuit described, that the territory thus allocated to one tribe was of great extent. <note n="145"> <div sID="gen23885" type="x-p"/> As originally laid out, it contained nearly a third of the whole Israelitish territory west of the Jordan. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen23885" type="x-p"/> </note> For although some diminution afterwards took place, its dominions always continued to be the largest.<div eID="gen23884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23886" type="x-p"/>It is necessary, however, to bear in mind what I formerly observed, that nothing else was determined by the lot than that the boundary of the children of Judah was to be contiguous to the land of Edom and the children of Sin, and that their boundary, in another direction, was to be the river of Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea — that those who had been selected to divide the country proceeded according to the best of their judgment, in proportioning the quantity of territory allotted to the number of their people, without extending their boundaries any farther — and that they followed the same method in other cases, as vicinity or other circumstances demanded.<div eID="gen23886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23887" type="x-p"/>Any error into which they fell, did not at all affect the general validity of their decision. For as they were not ashamed partly to recall any partition that might have been made without sufficient consideration, so the people in their turn, while they acknowledged that they had acted in the matter with the strictest good faith and honesty, submitted the more willingly to whatever they determined. Thus, notwithstanding any particular error, their general arrangements received full effect.<div eID="gen23887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23888" type="x-p"/>It will be worth while to make one remark on the city Jebus, whose name was afterwards Jerusalem. Although it had been already chosen, by the secret counsel of God, for his sanctuary, and the seat of the future kingdom, it however continued in the possession of the enemy down to the time of David. In this long exclusion from the place on which the sanctity, excellence, and glory of the rest of the land were founded, there was a clear manifestation of the divine curse inflicted to punish the people for their sluggishness: since it was virtually the same as if the land had been deprived of its principal dignity and ornament. But on the other hand, the wonderful goodness of God was conspicuous in this, that the Jebusites who, from the long respite which had been given them, seemed to have struck their roots most deeply, were at length torn up, and driven forth from their secure position.<div eID="gen23888" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen23881" osisID="Josh.15.1" type="section"/>
entries.dfc1d4c571caa17fd82b0b83f50b7471264bfeb8:
13. And unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh, etc Were we to judge from the actual state of matters, it would seem ridiculous repeatedly to celebrate an imaginary grant from which Caleb received no benefit while Joshua was alive. But herein due praise is given both to the truth of God, and to the faith of his saint in resting on his promise. Therefore, although sneering men, and the inhabitants of the place itself, if the rumor had reached them, might have derided the vain solicitude of Caleb, and the empty liberality of Joshua, the contempt thus expressed would only have proved them to be presumptuous scoffers. God at length evinced the firmness of his decree by the result, and Caleb, though he saw himself unable to obtain access to the mountain, testified that he was contented with the mere promise of God, the true exercise of faith, consisting in a willingness to remain without the fruition of things which have been promised till the period actually arrive. Moreover, this passage, and others similar to it, teach us that the giants who are usually called Enakim, were so named after their original progenitor, Enac, and that the word is hence of Gentile origin. The time when Caleb routed the sons of Enac we shall see in a short time. This passage also shows us that Caleb, when he brought forward the name of Moses, did not make a mere pretence, or utter anything that was not strictly true; for it is now plainly declared, that Moses had so appointed, in conformity with the command of God.
Joshua 15:14-63
14. And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
14. Expulit inde Caleb tres filios Enac, Sezadi, et Ahiman, et Thalmai qui fuerunt filii Enac.
15. And he went up thence to the inhabitants of Debir: and the name of Debir before was Kirjathsepher.
15. Ascenditque inde ad habitatores Debir, cujus nomen antea fuit Ciriath-sepher.
16. And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and takes it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.
16. Dixitque Caleb, qui percusserit Ciriath-sepher, et ceperit eam, dabo ei Achsa filiam meam in uxorem.
17. And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife.
17. Cepit autem eam Othniel filius Cenas fratris Caleb: deditque ei Achsa filiam suam in uxorem.
18. And it came to pass, as she came unto him, that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted off her ass; and Caleb said unto her, What would thou?
18. Fuitque quum veniret ipsa suasit illi, ut peteret a patre suo agrum, et descendit de asino, dixitque ei Caleb, Quid tibi est?
19. Who answered, Give me a blessing; for thou has given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs.
19. Illa respondit, Da mihi benedictionem: quandoquidem terram aridam dedisti mihi, da mihi fontes aquarum. Et dedit ei fontes superiores, et fontes inferiores.
20. ¶ This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families.

entries.79f5f04c87fd57be3055e73c0a716a74debfe5a7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.15.14" sID="gen23994" type="section"/> <div sID="gen23995" type="x-p"/>Here we have a narrative of what plainly appears from the book of Joshua to have taken place subsequent to the death of Joshua; but lest a question might have been raised by the novelty of the procedure, in giving a fertile and well watered field as the patrimony of a woman, the writer of the book thought proper to insert a history of that which afterwards happened, in order that no ambiguity might remain in regard to the lot of the tribe of Judah. First, Caleb is said, after he had taken the city of Hebron, to have attacked Debir or Ciriath-sepher, and to have declared, that the person who should be the first to enter it, would be his son-in-law. And it appears, that when he held out this rare prize to his fellow-soldiers for taking the city, no small achievement was required. This confirms what formerly seemed to be the case, that it was a dangerous and difficult task which had been assigned him, when he obtained his conditional grant. Accordingly, with the view of urging the bravest to exert themselves, he promises his daughter in marriage as a reward to the valor of the man who should first scale the wall.<div eID="gen23995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23996" type="x-p"/>It is afterwards added that Othniel who was his nephew by a brother, gained the prize by his valor. I know not how it has crept into the common translation that he was a younger brother of Caleb; for nothing in the least degree plausible can be said in defense of the blunder. Hence some expositors perplex themselves very unnecessarily in endeavoring to explain how Othniel could have married his niece, since such marriage was forbidden by the law. It is easy to see that he was not the uncle, but the cousin of his wife.<div eID="gen23996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23997" type="x-p"/>But here another question arises, How did Caleb presume to bargain concerning his daughter until he was made acquainted with her inclinations? <note n="146"> <div sID="gen23998" type="x-p"/> If we are to indulge in conjectures on the subject, this question might be answered by another, How do we know that Caleb had not consulted her inclinations, and instead of resting satisfied with the vague imaginings here ascribed to him, actually obtained her consent to the proposal which he was about to make? It may not have been, as Calvin supposes, a sudden thought which struck him in the heat of battle, but a calm resolve formed before he set out on his expedition against Debir, and intended to reward the most valiant of those who had assisted him in his war against the giants. And it is even not impossible that both he and his daughter, to whom Othniel, from his near relationship, must have been well known, had no doubt from the prowess he had previously exhibited, that he would outstrip all his competitors and carry off the prize. These, of course, are mere conjectures, but they are at least as plausible as those indulged in by other expositors, who, after raising the question, appear to have given themselves much unnecessary trouble in attempting to solve it. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen23998" type="x-p"/> </note> Although it is the office of parents to settle their daughters in life, they are not permitted to exercise tyrannical power and assign them to whatever husbands they think fit without consulting them. For while all contracts ought to be voluntary, freedom ought to prevail especially in marriage that no one may pledge his faith against his will. But Caleb was probably influenced by the belief that his daughter would willingly give her consent, as she could not modestly reject such honorable terms; <note n="147"> <div sID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pource qu’un tel partie et condition si honorable ne pouvoit estre refusee honnestement et sans impudence</foreign>;” “Because such a party and so honorable a condition could not be refused honestly (honorably) and without impudence.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> </note> for the husband to be given her was no common man, but one who should excel all others in warlike prowess. It is quite possible, however, that Caleb in the heat of battle inconsiderately promised what it was not in his power to perform. It seems to me, however, that according to common law, the agreement implied the daughter’s consent, and was only to take effect if it was obtained. <note n="148"> <div sID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> In other words, Caleb promises his daughter not absolutely to the man who should take the city, but to the man who, in addition to the prowess exerted in taking it, should also have the address to gain the daughter’s consent. It is difficult to believe that the promise made was either so meant by Caleb, or so interpreted by his followers. He very probably and, as the event showed, justly judged that his influence as a parent would either win or command his daughter’s consent. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> </note> God certainly heard the prayer of Caleb, when he gave him a son-in-law exactly to his mind. For had the free choice been given him, there was none whom he would have preferred.<div eID="gen23997" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen23994" osisID="Josh.15.14" type="section"/>
entries.9d08bcb118a386b4892d0a689a5cd7837beb5152: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.15.18" sID="gen24001" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi><hi type="italic"> And it came to pass as she came unto him, </hi>etc Although we may conjecture that the damsel Acsa was of excellent morals and well brought up, as marriage with her had been held forth as the special reward <note n="149"> <div sID="gen24003" type="x-p"/> French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour un salaire exquis et precieux</foreign>;” “As an exquisite and precious recompense.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24003" type="x-p"/> </note> of victory, yet perverse cupidity on her part is here disclosed. She knew that by the divine law women were specially excluded from hereditary lands, but she nevertheless covets the possession of them, and stimulates her husband by unjust expostulation. In this way ambitious and covetous wives cease not to molest their husbands until they force them to forget shame, modesty, and equity. For although the avarice of men also is insatiable, yet women are apt to be much more precipitate. The more carefully ought husbands to be on their guard against being set as it were on flame by the blast of such importunate counsels. <note n="150"> <div sID="gen24004" type="x-p"/> Latin, “<foreign xml:lang="la">Foeminae tamen magis praecipites feruntur</foreign>.” French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les femmes sont beaucoup plus bouillantes, et se laissent transporter plus aisement. Et d’autant plus sogneusement les maris se doyvent donner garde, de peur que par leurs conseils importuns, qui sont comme des soufflets, ils ne soyent embrasez</foreign>;” “Women are much more fervid, and allow themselves to be more easily carried away. And so much the more carefully should husbands be on their guard, lest by their importunate counsels, which are like bellows, they be blown into flame.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24004" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen24002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24005" type="x-p"/>But a greater degree of intemperance is displayed when she acquires additional boldness from the facility of her husband and the indulgence of her father. Not contented with the field given to her, she demands for herself a well-watered district. And thus it is when a person has once overleaped the bounds of rectitude and honesty, the fault is forthwith followed up by impudence. Moreover, her father in refusing her nothing gives proof of his singular affection for her. But it does not therefore follow that the wicked thirst of gain which blinds the mind and perverts right judgment is the less hateful. In regard to Acsa’s dismounting from the ass, some interpreters ascribe it to dissimulation and craft, as if she were pretending inability to retain her seat from grief. In this way her dismounting or falling off is made an indication of criminality and defective character. It is more simple, however, to suppose that she placed herself at her father’s feet with the view of accosting him as a suppliant. Be this as it may, by her craft and flattery she gained his consent, and in so far diminished the portion of her brothers. <note n="151"> <div sID="gen24006" type="x-p"/> French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quoy qu’il en soit, cette femme attira a soy par astuce et flatteries le droit d’autruy, et par ce moyen, la part et portion de ses freres en fut d’autant amoindrie</foreign>;” “Be this as it may, this woman attracted to herself by craft and flattery the right of another, and by this means the part and portion of her brothers was so far lessened.” The censure here passed upon Achsah is rather more severe than the circumstances seem to warrant. It ought to be remembered, that in cases of succession the preference given to males is only conventional, and that by natural law her brothers’ title was not a whit better than her own. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24006" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen24005" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24001" osisID="Josh.15.18" type="section"/>
entries.c51d63b6f787bbae7bc5016366f3e6d7b2e2f4b9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.15.20" sID="gen24007" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">This is the inheritance, </hi>etc He had formerly, indeed, traced out the boundaries of the children of Judah; but it is now shown for a different reason how large and fertile the territory was which the Lord in his great liberality had bestowed upon them. One hundred and thirteen cities with their towns and villages are enumerated. The number attests not only the populousness, but also the fertility of the country. And there cannot be a doubt that by the divine blessing a new degree of fertility was imparted to it. The goodness of God was, however, manifested in the very nature of the land selected for his people, a land abounding in all kinds of advantages. If we attend to the number of souls in the tribe, we shall find that one half of the country would have been amply sufficient for their habitation. For when eight hundred were allocated in each of the cities, the remainder had the towns and the villages. It is no doubt true that a portion was afterwards withdrawn and given to the tribe of Simeon. For in this was accomplished the dispersion of which Jacob had prophesied,<div eID="gen24008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24009" type="x-p"/>“I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.7">Genesis 49:7</reference>)<div eID="gen24009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24010" type="x-p"/>They were accordingly admitted by the children of Judah as a kind of guests.<div eID="gen24010" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.15.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24007" osisID="Josh.15.20" type="section"/>

As for the Jebusites, etc This furnishes no excuse for the people, nor is it set down with that view; for had they exerted themselves to the full measure of their strength, and failed of success, the dishonor would have fallen on God himself, who had promised that he would continue with them as their leader until he should give them full and free possession of the land, and that he would send hornets to drive out the inhabitants. Therefore, it was owing entirely to their own sluggishness that they did not make themselves masters of the city of Jerusalem. This they were not able to do; but their own torpor, their neglect of the divine command from a love of ease, were the real obstacles.
This passage is deserving of notice: we ought to learn from it to make vigorous trial of our strength in attempting to accomplish the commands of God, and not to omit any opportunity, lest while we are idly resting the door may be shut. A moderate delay might have been free from blame; but a long period of effeminate ease in a manner rejected the blessing which God was ready to bestow.
Some of the Jewish expositors, unwilling to admit the cowardice and sluggishness of their countrymen, fable that the Jebusites were permitted to remain in possession because they were descendants of Abimelech, and in consequence of the covenant made between him and Abraham, (Genesis 21:22, 32,) could not be lawfully expelled. — Ed.
CHAPTER 16
Joshua 16:1-10
1. And the lot of the children of Joseph fell from Jordan by Jericho, unto the water of Jericho on the east, to the wilderness that goeth up from Jericho throughout mount Bethel,
1. Egressa est autem sors filiis Joseph a Jordane Jericho, ad aquas Jericho ad orientem, ad desertum quod ascendit a Jericho in montem Beth-el.
2. And goeth out from Bethel to Luz, and passes along unto the borders of Archi to Ataroth,
2. Egrediturque a Beth-el in Luz, et hinc pertransit ad terminum Archi-Atoroth.
3. And goeth down westward to the coast of Japhleti, unto the coast of Bethhoron the nether, and to Gezer: and the goings out thereof are at the sea.
3. Postea ascendit ad mare, ad terminum Japhleti usque ad terminum Beth-horon inferiorem et usque ad Gazer, suntque exitus ejus ad mare.
4. So the children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance.
4. Itaque haereditatem acceperunt ilii Joseph, Manasses et Ephraim.
5. And the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families was thus: even the border of their inheritance on the east side was Atarothaddar, unto Bethhoron the upper;
5. Fuit autem terminus filiorum Ephraim per familias suas: fuitinquam, terminus haereditatis eorum ad orientem ab Atroh-Addar, usque ad Beth-horon superiorem.
6. And the border went out toward the sea to Michmethah on the north side; and the border went about eastward unto Taanathshiloh, and passed by it on the east to Janohah;
6. Et exit terminus ille ad mare, ad Michmethah ab aquilone: et circumit terminus ad orientem, ad Thaanath-siloh, et transit illam ab oriente ad Janoah.

7. Et descendit a Janoah in Ataroth, et Naarath, et pervenit in Jericho, egrediturque ad Jordanem.

8. A Thappuah pergit terminus ad mare ad torrentem arundinis, suntque exitus ejus ad mare, haec est hereditas tribus filiorum Ephraim per familias suas.
9. And the separate cities for the children of Ephraim were among the inheritance of the children of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages.
9. Et urbes separatae filiis Ephraim in medio haereditatis filiorum Manasse, omnes urbes, et villae earum.

                     </ns0:gap>em <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For though <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was in part taken by <ns0:hi>Ioshua</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore this; yet the upper and stronger part of it, called <ns0:hi>Zi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on,</ns0:hi> was still kept by the <ns0:hi>Iebusites,</ns0:hi> even until <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> time; and it seems from thence they descended to the lower Town called <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and took it; so that the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were forced to win it a second time; yea, and a third time also: for afterwards it was possessed by the <ns0:hi>Iebusites, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 19. 11. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 5. 6, 7.</ns0:note>, the children of Judah could not drive them out <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Namely, because of their unbe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief, as Christ <ns0:hi>could do no mighty work—because of the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples unbelief,</ns0:hi> Mark 6. 5, 6. Mat. 13. 58. and because of their Sloth, and Cowardise, and Wickedness, whereby they for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feited Gods help, and then they must needs be imporent; but this inability was wilful, and brought upon them by them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves.</ns0:note>: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The same things which are here said of the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> are said of the <ns0:hi>Benjamites, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1. 21. Hence ariseth a question, To which of the Tribes <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> belonged? whether to <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> as is gathered from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 27. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 12. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 6. 1. or to <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> as is implied here, and <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 78. 68, 69. Some think, that being in the Borders of both, it was common to both, and promiscu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ously inhabited by both; and it is certain, that after the Cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tivity it was possessed by both, <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 11. 4. But for the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent, though it did belong to <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> yet the Children of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> being possibly very active in the first taking of it by <ns0:hi>Ioshua,</ns0:hi> as they certainly were after his Death, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. they might thereby get some right to share with the <ns0:hi>Ben<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jamites</ns0:hi> in the Possession of it. It seems most probable, that part of it, and indeed the greatest part, and main bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy of it, stood in the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Benjamin;</ns0:hi> and hence this is mentioned in the List of their Cities, and not in <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi>'s List; and part of it stood in <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi>'s share, even Mount <ns0:hi>Moriah,</ns0:hi> on which the Temple was built; and Mount <ns0:hi>Sion,</ns0:hi> when it was taken from the <ns0:hi>Iebusites.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> unto this day <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">When this Book was written, whether in <ns0:hi>Ioshuah</ns0:hi>'s Life and Old Age, which continued many years after the taking of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem;</ns0:hi> or after his Death, when this Clause was added here and elsewhere in this Book by some other man of God, which must needs be done be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> time, when the <ns0:hi>Iebusites</ns0:hi> were quite expelled, and their Fort taken.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
